title: Why Didn't Viking Helmets Have Horns?
description:
Say "Vikings" and many people picture a horned helmet. This episode covers only what the records show. In 1943 a farmer's son in Ringerike, Norway, dug up a grave from the late 10th century; its Gjermundbu helmet is iron, with "spectacles" guarding the eyes and nose, and no horns. Only two nearly complete Viking helmets are known from Scandinavia and Britain, and no known Viking Age helmet or fragment has horns; the court poem from the same century and the history written around 1225 that we read don't mention horns either. The Viksø helmets, which do have horns, came out of a Danish bog in 1942; a 2021 study dates them to about 900 BC, some 1,700 years before the Viking Age. The horns were borrowed later: in 1616 a scholar gave horns to the early Germans; at the first complete Ring of the Nibelung in Bayreuth in 1876, Carl Emil Doepler put horns on some warriors and attendants, and that opera has no Vikings in it; the first eight illustrated editions of the novel Erling the Bold showed wings, and horns first appeared in the ninth edition, in 1890.

Limits: what the Viksø helmets were used for is the interpretation of the museum and researchers; Cosima Wagner and Montelius are quoted via Roberta Frank; "horns are impractical" is the view of Norway's Museum of the Viking Age; the horned helmet had no single inventor. Sources are listed in the references below.

Illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters, not likenesses. Modern researchers are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-20

vk101.text: Spring 1943, Ringerike, Norway: a farmer's son was building a house for his parents.

vk102.text: On the afternoon of March 29, leveling a mound, he dug something up:

vk104.text: Among the finds, an iron helmet in nine pieces.

vk105.text: But it lacked the thing everyone expects to see: horns.

vk107.text: A year earlier, bog workers in Denmark dug up two helmets;

vk109.text: In 1872, a Swedish archaeologist wrote down what a tiny figure wore on its head.

vk110.text: In summer 1876, on an opera stage in Bayreuth, Germany, someone put on horns;

vk112.text: A museum gift shop in America ran into trouble.

vk113.text: Why didn't Viking helmets have horns?

vk201.text: Two days later the hornless iron helmet was in the local paper: the paper said it had "spectacles."

vk203.text: Pieced together, it's a round iron cap with a small spike on top;

vk204.text: an iron frame shields eyes and nose, like a pair of glasses.

vk205.text: Small iron rings on the rim once held mail to protect the neck.

vk206.text: Complete, it weighed about 1.5 kg, like a modern soldier's helmet.

vk207.text: It's named after the farm: the Gjermundbu helmet.

vk208.text: The same grave held a sword, two spears, two axes and riding gear;

vk209.text: the grave dates to the late 10th century.

vk210.text: Oddly, the helmet had been damaged on purpose.

vk211.text: The grave's two spears each pierced it once;

vk212.text: the museum calls it part of the burial rite.

vk213.text: Few warriors could afford such a helmet.

vk215.text: In Scandinavia and Britain, only two are nearly complete, plus a few fragments.

vk216.text: The other turned up in Yarm, England, during sewer work in the 1950s;

vk217.text: a 2020 study judged it Viking Age; it too has spectacles over the face.

vk218.text: To this day, no Viking Age helmet or fragment has horns.

vk219.text: Did writers of the time ever give helmets horns?

vk220.text: We read a Norwegian court poem from the same century, Hákonarmál:

vk221.text: it has golden helmets and helmeted Valkyries, but no horns.

vk222.text: Then Heimskringla, a history written around 1225, mentions helmets dozens of times:

vk223.text: with nose guards, gilded, painted with crosses, and not one with horns.

vk224.text: So who wore those two horned Danish helmets?

vk301.text: Not Vikings. They went into the bog around 900 BC.

vk302.text: A 2021 study dated them from a bit of birch tar on one horn.

vk303.text: That's about 1,700 years before the Viking Age.

vk304.text: That peat cutter was working in 1942 at Viksø, on Zealand, Denmark,

vk305.text: when something crunched under his spade.

vk306.text: He took it for buried rubbish and set it aside.

vk307.text: Two nearly identical bronze helmets: besides a pair of horns, they had eyes and a hooked beak.

vk308.text: They may have sported horsehair and feathers too.

vk309.text: Were horns that big worn into battle?

vk310.text: The National Museum of Denmark says no: they were for rituals;

vk311.text: part of a priest's costume, it says, later given to the bog as offerings.

vk312.text: A Danish archaeologist who studies them puts it bluntly:

vk313.text: linking them to the Vikings is nonsense.

vk314.text: So did these two inspire the 19th century's horned Vikings?

vk315.text: Impossible. Remember that stage in Bayreuth?

vk316.text: These two were found 66 years after that stage.

vk317.text: What people then could see: tiny figures on helmet plates.

vk318.text: In 1870, four bronze dies for stamping helmet plates were found on Öland, Sweden,

vk320.text: One shows a dancer with weapons, two curved things rising from his head.

vk322.text: That Swedish archaeologist published these dies in 1872;

vk323.text: he wrote: a helmet with two projections, two bird necks facing each other.

vk325.text: Frank, a scholar of this history, says it mostly went the other way:

vk326.text: they pictured horned Vikings first, then saw horns in old finds.

vk327.text: So where did the horned idea come from?

vk401.text: From older books. In 1875, Wagner's costume designer Doepler had an opera to dress;

vk402.text: he opened the Roman Tacitus's book on the Germans and its commentaries.

vk403.text: Yet Tacitus wrote that hardly one or two Germans had a metal helmet or leather cap.

vk404.text: The horns were borrowed: an ancient historian wrote that many Gaulish helmets bore horns.

vk405.text: In 1616, a geographer cited these old texts and put horns on the early Germans.

vk406.text: Those were the horns Doepler found in the commentaries.

vk407.text: Before that, what did Vikings wear in paintings?

vk409.text: Most 18th-century Vikings in art wore winged helmets.

vk410.text: In 1869, London saw a novel of Norse sea kings, Erling the Bold;

vk412.text: The book says a pair of hawk's wings rose from his steel helmet.

vk413.text: In August 1876, the Bayreuth Festival Theatre opened with the first complete Ring of the Nibelung.

vk414.text: That stage held gods, dwarfs, giants and heroes of myth, and not a single Viking.

vk415.text: Doepler gave horns to some of the warriors and attendants;

vk416.text: yet the Valkyrie got a white winged helmet.

vk417.text: Wagner's wife Cosima even complained the costumes recalled "Indian chiefs."

vk418.text: So how did horns end up on Vikings?

vk419.text: Book by book. Frithiof, hero of a Swedish epic poem, mostly wore an "eagle helm" in pictures;

vk420.text: only in the late 1870s did a popular book give him horns.

vk421.text: Erling the Bold: all eight illustrated editions before 1880 showed wings;

vk422.text: in the ninth edition, in 1890, horns appeared for the first time.

vk423.text: In art books, children's books and ads, Viking after Viking got horns;

vk424.text: Frank says that by the 1890s, horned Vikings were like the weather: everywhere.

vk425.text: The Vikings' homeland was slowest. Remember Heimskringla?

vk426.text: In its 1899 Norwegian translation, the Vikings wear only conical helmets, row after boring row.

vk427.text: But Frank also says the horned helmet had no single source.

vk428.text: By 1900, the horns had become the Viking trademark.

vk501.text: No. In 1961, the Minnesota Vikings played their first season,

vk502.text: with horns painted on the sides of their helmets.

vk504.text: For a Smithsonian Viking show, the shop struggled to order Viking goods without horns.

vk505.text: So why did that iron helmet in nine pieces have no horns?

vk506.text: It never lacked anything; the horns were put on Vikings later, in the 19th century.

vk508.text: Where did you first see a horned Viking: a cartoon, a game or a storybook?

vk509.text: This channel covers only what is on record. Subscribe to open the files.
